text: The Mississippi River is the primary river of the largest drainage basin in the United States, the second-longest river in the country after the Missouri, and the world's tenth-largest by discharge flow and the largest in North America. It flows from its traditional source at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, 1,475 feet (450 m) above sea level, to the Gulf of Mexico over a distance of 2,340 miles (3,770 km), with a stream gradient of 0.01% and a total drop of 450 meters over 3,766 km. The river's watershed covers 1,151,000 square miles (2,980,000 km²), including all or parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces, and accounts for nearly 40% of the continental U.S. landmass. The highest point in the watershed is Mount Elbert at 14,440 feet (4,400 m), in the Rocky Mountains. The river's average annual discharge ranges between 200,000 and 700,000 cubic feet per second (6,000 to 20,000 m³/s), with a long-term mean discharge at Cairo, Illinois, of 281,500 cu ft/s (7,970 m³/s) from the Ohio River and 208,200 cu ft/s (5,900 m³/s) from the Mississippi. The river's flow is 8% that of the Amazon, which averages nearly 7 million cubic feet per second during wet seasons. Before 1900, the Mississippi transported an estimated 440 million short tons (400 million metric tons) of sediment annually; this has decreased to 160 million short tons (145 million metric tons) per year due to engineering modifications such as dams, meander cutoffs, and bank revetments. The river is divided into three sections: the Upper Mississippi, from Lake Itasca to the Missouri River confluence at St. Louis, Missouri; the Middle Mississippi, from St. Louis to the Ohio River confluence at Cairo, Illinois, covering 190 miles (310 km) and dropping 220 feet (67 m) over 180 miles (290 km); and the Lower Mississippi, from the Ohio River to the Gulf of Mexico, about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) long. The Upper Mississippi is regulated by 43 dams, including 14 above Minneapolis and 29 downstream, with locks and dams designed to improve navigation and manage flow. The head of navigation is currently at Minneapolis after the Coon Rapids Dam, though the St. Anthony Falls Lock and Dam, completed in 1963, previously held that position until 2015 when it was closed to prevent the spread of invasive Asian carp. The river's elevation drops from 799 feet (244 m) above sea level above the St. Anthony Falls Dam to 750 feet (230 m) below, a 49-foot (15 m) drop—the largest of any lock and dam on the Mississippi. The Upper Mississippi includes major tributaries such as the Minnesota, St. Croix, Cannon, Zumbro, Black, La Crosse, Root, Wisconsin, Rock, Iowa, Skunk, and Des Moines rivers. The river is a multi-thread stream with natural and artificial lakes, including Lake Winnibigoshish (over 11 miles wide), Lake Onalaska (over 4 miles wide), and Lake Pepin (over 2 miles wide). The Middle Mississippi is relatively free-flowing, with no major tributaries except the Missouri and Meramec rivers. The Lower Mississippi receives major tributaries including the White, Arkansas, Big Black, and Yazoo rivers. The river's flow is diverted at the Old River Control Structure in Louisiana, where 30% of the combined flow of the Mississippi and Red Rivers goes to the Gulf via the Atchafalaya River instead of continuing down the main channel to New Orleans. The river's mouth is located about 100 miles (160 km) downstream from New Orleans, and the average speed is about 26 miles (42 km) per day or 1 mile (1.6 km) per hour. The river's retention time from Lake Itasca to the Gulf is about 90 days. The lower Mississippi has undergone repeated avulsion events every thousand years due to sediment buildup, shifting its course and forming abandoned distributaries known as bayous, which have advanced the Louisiana coastline by 15 to 50 miles (24 to 80 km) over the past 5,000 years. The current active delta is known as the Birdfoot or Balize Delta. The river's basin was shaped by the Laurentide Ice Sheet during the most recent Ice Age and by geological processes including the formation of the Reelfoot Rift around 80 million years ago due to crustal subsidence after uplift from a volcanic hotspot. The river's water flows into the Gulf of Mexico, forming a distinct plume visible in NASA MODIS images that remains separate from salt water for a long distance before mixing, and in drought years, saltwater can travel up to 64 miles (103 km) upstream, contaminating drinking water, prompting the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to construct saltwater sills in 1988, 1999, 2012, and 2022 to contain it. The name "Mississippi" comes from the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe or Algonquin) term Misi-ziibi (Great River), rendered in French as Misi zipi. The river served as a border in the 18th century under the Treaty of Paris and later became a key boundary in the Louisiana Purchase and westward expansion, symbolized by the Gateway Arch in St. Louis and the Trans-Mississippi Exposition. The river is also used as a dividing line for broadcast call signs, with W to the east and K to the west, and regional landmarks are often classified relative to it, such as "the highest peak east of the Mississippi" or "the oldest city west of the Mississippi." The river is commonly nicknamed "The Mighty Mississippi River" or simply "The Mighty Mississippi."

The Mississippi River originates at Lake Itasca and is approximately 2,340 miles (3,766 km) long when measured from its traditional source, making it the fourth longest river in the world after the Nile, Amazon, and Yangtze. When measured from its longest stream source, Brower's Spring in Montana (the headwaters of the Missouri River), the river is 3,710 miles (5,971 km) long. When measured from the largest stream source by water volume—the Ohio River and its tributary, the Allegheny River—the Mississippi begins in Pennsylvania. At its source, the river is about 3 feet (0.91 m) deep; between Saint Paul and Saint Louis, the average depth is 9 to 12 feet (2.7–3.7 m), with Lake Pepin averaging 20–32 feet (6–10 m) and reaching a maximum depth of 60 feet (18 m). Between Saint Louis and Cairo, Illinois, the depth averages 30 feet (9 m), and below Cairo, where the Ohio River joins, it averages 50–100 feet (15–30 m), with the deepest point in New Orleans reaching 200 feet (61 m). The river flows through or along 10 states, from Minnesota to Louisiana, and defines portions of their borders, with Wisconsin, Illinois, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi on the east side and Iowa, Missouri, and Arkansas on the west. State borders are based on the middle of the riverbed at the time they were established, and despite shifts in the river’s course, the borders remain unchanged, leaving small isolated areas of one state across the new channel. The river’s course has changed dramatically over time due to natural processes such as avulsion, which occurs roughly every thousand years when sediment buildup raises the river’s level, prompting it to find a steeper, more direct route to the Gulf of Mexico. This process has advanced the coastline of south Louisiana by 15 to 50 miles (24 to 80 km) over the past 5,000 years. The current active delta lobe is known as the Birdfoot Delta or the Balize Delta, named after La Balize, Louisiana, the first French settlement at the river’s mouth. The river’s basin was shaped by the Laurentide Ice Sheet during the most recent Ice Age, with the southernmost extent of the ice sheet extending into present-day U.S. and the Mississippi basin. As the ice sheet retreated, hundreds of feet of rich sediment were deposited, forming the flat, fertile landscape of the Mississippi Valley. During the melt, glacial rivers established drainage paths into the Mississippi watershed, creating valleys such as the Minnesota, James, and Milk Rivers. After the ice sheet fully retreated, many of these rivers found paths to Hudson Bay or the Arctic Ocean, leaving the basin with features larger than what the existing rivers could have carved in the same time period. During the Illinoian Stage (300,000 to 132,000 years before present), the ice sheet blocked the Mississippi near Rock Island, Illinois, diverting it to its present western channel, which now forms the border of Illinois. The Hennepin Canal follows the ancient Mississippi channel from Rock Island to Hennepin, Illinois, and the current Illinois River follows the old Mississippi path from Hennepin to Alton, Illinois. In March 1876, the river suddenly changed course near Reverie, Tennessee, leaving a small part of Tipton County, Tennessee, attached to Arkansas and separated from the rest of Tennessee, but the state line still follows the old channel. The town of Kaskaskia, Illinois, once stood on a peninsula at the confluence of the Mississippi and Kaskaskia (Okaw) Rivers, serving as a French colonial community, the capital of the Illinois Territory, and the first state capital of Illinois until 1819. Starting in 1844, repeated flooding caused the river to slowly encroach eastward, and a major flood in 1881 overtook the lower 10 miles (16 km) of the Kaskaskia River, forming a new channel and cutting off the town. Later floods destroyed most of the town, including the original State House. Today, a remaining 2,300 acres (930 ha) island with 14 residents is known as an enclave of Illinois and is accessible only from Missouri. The New Madrid Seismic Zone, along the Mississippi near New Madrid, Missouri, is linked to an aulacogen (failed rift) that formed with the Gulf of Mexico and remains seismically active. Four major earthquakes in 1811 and 1812, estimated at 8 on the Richter scale, caused significant local damage and were felt widely across the Midwest and eastern U.S., creating Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee. The earliest bridge across the Mississippi was built in 1855 in Minneapolis, where the current Hennepin Avenue Bridge stands. The first railroad bridge was constructed in 1856 between the Rock Island Arsenal and Davenport, Iowa; it was attacked by the steamboat Effie Afton, which set it on fire, leading to a Supreme Court ruling in favor of the railroad. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, established in 1802, is responsible for maintaining a navigation channel, beginning with early surveys in 1829 of the Des Moines Rapids and Rock Island Rapids, both of which were considered impassable. The Corps recommended a 5-foot-deep channel at the Des Moines Rapids, which began in 1837, and later excavated the Rock Island Rapids. By 1866, excavation was deemed impractical, leading to the construction of a canal around the Des Moines Rapids, which opened in 1877, while the Rock Island Rapids remained an obstacle. In 1878, Congress authorized a 4.5-foot-deep channel via wing dams, and the Moline Lock, bypassing the Rock Island Rapids, opened in 1907. In 1907, Congress authorized a 6-foot-deep channel project, which was abandoned in the late 1920s in favor of a 9-foot-deep (2.7 m) channel. Lock and Dam No. 19 at Keokuk, Iowa, completed in 1913, was built by the Union Electric Company to generate electricity and eliminated the Des Moines Rapids. Lock and Dam No. 1 in Minneapolis was completed in 1917, and Lock and Dam No. 2 near Hastings in 1930. Before the 1927 flood, the Corps aimed to close side channels to increase main river flow, believing this would deepen the river and reduce flooding; the 1927 flood disproved this, leading communities to create their own levee breaks. The Rivers and Harbors Act of 1930 authorized the 9-foot-deep, 400-foot-wide navigation channel, achieved through 23 new locks and dams built in the 1930s. Until the 1950s, there was no dam below Lock and Dam 26 at Alton, Illinois; Chain of Rocks Lock (No. 27), added in 1953, bypasses rock ledges at St. Louis and protects city water intakes. In the 1950s, scientists determined the Mississippi was shifting to the Atchafalaya River due to its steeper path to the Gulf, prompting Congress to authorize the Old River Control Structure to prevent the river from switching to the Atchafalaya and leaving New Orleans on a side channel. An auxiliary flow control station was built in 1986 for the $300 million project. Dam 26 at Alton was replaced by the Mel Price Lock and Dam in 1990, and the original dam was demolished. The Corps now maintains spillways and floodways, including the Birds Point-New Madrid Floodway in Missouri, the Old River Control Structure and Morganza Spillway in Louisiana (directing water to the west and east sides of the Atchafalaya), and the Bonnet Carré Spillway (directing water to Lake Pontchartrain), to divert floodwaters and reduce pressure on New Orleans and Baton Rouge. Some pre-1927 strategies, such as cutting the necks of horseshoe bends, are still used to reduce flood heights. Approximately 50,000 years ago, the Central United States was covered by an inland sea, drained by the Mississippi and its tributaries into the Gulf of Mexico, creating large floodplains and extending the continent southward, resulting in rich soils in areas like Louisiana. The Mississippi basin was first inhabited by Native American peoples who practiced hunting and gathering and are considered one of the few independent centers of plant domestication in human history. Evidence of early cultivation of sunflower, goosefoot, marsh elder, and indigenous squash dates to the 4th millennium BC. After about 1000 BC, during the Woodland period, lifestyles became more settled with shelter construction, pottery, and weaving. From 200 to 500 AD, the Hopewell interaction sphere facilitated trade and cultural exchange across the region. After 800 AD, agriculture introduced from Mesoamerica, based on the Three Sisters (maize, beans, and squash), became dominant, leading to the rise of the Mississippian culture, characterized by complex chiefdoms and large population centers. The most prominent site, Cahokia, was occupied between 600 and 1400 AD, with a peak population of 8,000 to 40,000—larger than London at the time—and was later dispersed, with archaeological evidence indicating increased social stress at first contact with Europeans. Modern American Indian nations in the Mississippi basin include Cheyenne, Sioux, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Ho-Chunk, and Meskwaki.

The Hopewell interaction sphere was active between 200 and 500 AD, spreading common cultural practices across waterways from the Gulf of Mexico to the Great Lakes. After this period, communities became more isolated, and agriculture based on the Three Sisters—maize, beans, and squash—introduced from Mesoamerica gradually became dominant. Around 800 AD, an advanced agricultural society known as the Mississippian culture emerged, characterized by highly stratified chiefdoms and large population centers. The most prominent site, Cahokia, was occupied between 600 and 1400 AD and had a population between 8,000 and 40,000 at its peak, larger than London at the time. At first contact with Europeans, Cahokia and other Mississippian cities had dispersed, and archaeological evidence indicates increased social stress. Modern American Indian nations in the Mississippi basin include Cheyenne, Sioux, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Ho-Chunk, Meskwaki, Kickapoo, Tamaroa, Moingwena, Quapaw, and Chickasaw. The name "Mississippi" comes from Messipi, the French version of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe or Algonquin) name Misi-ziibi (Great River). The Ojibwe refer to Lake Itasca as Omashkoozo-zaaga'igan (Elk Lake) and the river from it as Omashkoozo-ziibi (Elk River); after flowing into Lake Bemidji, it is called Bemijigamaag-ziibi (River from the Traversing Lake); into Cass Lake, Gaa-miskwaawaakokaag-ziibi (Red Cedar River); out of Lake Winnibigoshish, Wiinibiigoonzhish-ziibi (Miserable Wretched Dirty Water River); after merging with the Leech Lake River, Gichi-ziibi (Big River); and finally Misi-ziibi (Great River) after the Crow Wing River confluence. After Giacomo Beltrami and Henry Schoolcraft's expeditions, the longest stream above the Crow Wing and Gichi-ziibi confluence was named the "Mississippi River." The Mississippi River Band of Chippewa Indians, known as the Gichi-ziibiwininiwag, are named after the Gichi-ziibi stretch. The Cheyenne called it Máʼxe-éʼometaaʼe (Big Greasy River), the Arapaho named it Beesniicíe, and the Pawnee called it Kickaátit. During French Louisiana, the river was spelled Mississipi or Missisipi and also known as the Rivière Saint-Louis. In 1519, Alonso Álvarez de Pineda was the first recorded European to reach the river; Hernando de Soto reached it on May 8, 1541, calling it Río del Espíritu Santo in present-day Mississippi, and in Spanish it is called Río Mississippi. Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette explored the river in the 17th century; Marquette traveled with a Sioux guide who named it Ne Tongo ("Big river") in 1673, and Marquette proposed calling it the River of the Immaculate Conception. When Jolliet explored the valley, natives guided him to the Chicago Portage, which he noted required only a canal of "half a league" (less than 2 miles or 3 kilometers) to connect the Mississippi and Great Lakes. In 1848, the Illinois and Michigan canal breached the continental divide between the Great Lakes and Mississippi Valley, accelerating development and permanently altering the region's ecology. In 1682, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, and Henri de Tonti claimed the entire Mississippi River valley for France, naming it the Colbert River and the region La Louisiane for King Louis XIV. On March 2, 1699, Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville rediscovered the river's mouth after La Salle's death and built the small fort of La Balise to control passage. In 1718, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, established New Orleans about 100 miles upriver, modeled after Mobile. In 1727, Étienne Perier began constructing the first levees on the river using enslaved African laborers. After Britain's victory in the Seven Years War, the Mississippi became the border between British and Spanish territories; the Treaty of Paris (1763) granted Britain all land east of the river and Spain all land west of it, with Spain ceding Florida to Britain to regain Cuba. Britain then divided the territory into East and West Florida. Article 8 of the Treaty of Paris (1783) stated that navigation of the Mississippi from its source to the ocean would remain free and open to British subjects and U.S. citizens. Britain ceded West Florida back to Spain to regain the Bahamas, and initial disputes were resolved when Spain signed Pinckney's Treaty in 1795. In 1800, under pressure from Napoleon, Spain secretly ceded an undefined portion of West Florida to France in the Treaty of San Ildefonso. The United States secured effective control of the river through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. A dispute arose over which parts of West Florida Spain had ceded to France, affecting which areas the U.S. acquired in the purchase. Due to U.S. colonization and military actions, Spain ceded both West and East Florida to the United States in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819. The last serious European challenge to U.S. control came at the end of the War of 1812, when British forces attacked New Orleans just 15 days after the Treaty of Ghent was signed, but were repelled by General Andrew Jackson. In the 1818 Treaty between the U.S. and Great Britain, the border from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains was set along the 49th parallel, effectively transferring the northwestern extremity of the Mississippi basin to Britain in exchange for the southern portion of the Red River basin. Zadok Cramer wrote a guidebook, The Navigator, detailing the river's features, dangers, and navigable waterways, which was updated and expanded into 12 editions over 25 years. The colonization of the area was not significantly slowed by three earthquakes in 1811 and 1812, estimated at 8 on the Richter scale, centered near New Madrid, Missouri. Mark Twain's book, Life on the Mississippi, covered steamboat commerce from 1830 to 1870, first published as a seven-part serial in Harper's Weekly in 1875 and fully published by James R. Osgood & Company in 1885, including a passage from the unfinished Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. The first steamboat to travel the full length of the Lower Mississippi from the Ohio River to New Orleans was the New Orleans, which made its maiden voyage during the 1811–12 New Madrid earthquakes. The Upper Mississippi was treacherous and poorly mapped, with only two steamboat trips per year to the Twin Cities landings until the 1840s, indicating limited profitability. In 1851, Secretary of War Charles M. Conrad authorized a scientific study of the river to prevent flooding, first published in 1861 as "Report upon the Physics and Hydraulics of the Mississippi River," the most extensive river study of its time. Steamboat transport remained viable for passengers and freight until the end of the first decade of the 20th century. The Anchor Line operated a luxurious fleet between St. Louis and New Orleans from 1859 to 1898. Giacomo Beltrami wrote about his journey on the Virginia, the first steamboat to reach Fort St. Anthony in Minnesota, describing it as a promenade once a journey. The steamboat era transformed the economic and political life of the Mississippi and introduced a flourishing tourist trade. Control of the river was a strategic objective in the American Civil War, part of the U.S. Anaconda Plan. In 1862, Union forces cleared Confederate defenses at Island Number 10 and Memphis, Tennessee, and naval forces captured New Orleans, Louisiana. The last major Confederate stronghold was at Vicksburg, Mississippi; the Union's Vicksburg Campaign (December 1862–July 1863) and the fall of Port Hudson completed control of the lower Mississippi River. The Union victory ended the Siege of Vicksburg on July 4, 1863, and was pivotal to the Union's final victory. The "Big Freeze" of 1918–19 blocked river traffic north of Memphis, Tennessee, preventing coal transport from southern Illinois, leading to widespread shortages, high prices, and rationing in January and February. In spring 1927, the river broke out in 145 places during the Great Mississippi Flood, inundating 27,000 mi² (70,000 km²) to a depth of up to 30 feet (9.1 m). In 1930, Fred Newton became the first person to swim the river from Minneapolis to New Orleans, completing the 1,836-mile journey in 176 days. In 1962 and 1963, industrial accidents spilled 3.5 million U.S. gallons (13,000 m³) of soybean oil into the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers, covering the Mississippi from St. Paul to Lake Pepin and causing an ecological disaster and a demand for pollution control. On October 20, 1976, the MV George Prince ferry was struck by a ship while crossing from Destrehan to Luling, Louisiana, resulting in 78 deaths and 18 survivors. In 1988, the water level at the Memphis gauge dropped to 10 feet (3.0 m) below zero, exposing wooden-hulled craft from the late 19th to early 20th centuries over 4.5 acres (1.8 ha) in West Memphis, Arkansas. The State of Arkansas, the Arkansas Archeological Survey, and the Arkansas Archeological Society conducted a two-month data recovery effort, receiving national media attention during a drought. The Great Flood of 1993 primarily affected the Mississippi above its confluence with the Ohio River at Cairo, Illinois. Two portions of the Mississippi were designated American Heritage Rivers in 1997: the lower portion around Louisiana and Tennessee, and the upper portion around Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, Missouri, and Wisconsin. The Nature Conservancy's "America's Rivershed Initiative" released a report card in October 2015, giving the basin a grade of D+, noting aging infrastructure and multiple environmental problems. In 2002, Slovenian swimmer Martin Strel swam the entire river from Minnesota to Louisiana in 68 days. In 2005, the Source to Sea Expedition paddled the Mississippi and Atchafalaya Rivers to support the Audubon Society's Upper Mississippi River Campaign. Geologists believe the lower Mississippi could take a new course to the Gulf via either the Atchafalaya Basin or Lake Pontchartrain if flood-control structures are overtopped or damaged. A failure of the Old River Control Structure between the Mississippi and Atchafalaya Basin could divert 30% of the river's flow to the Atchafalaya River, with a steep drop into the basin. If the structure fails during a major flood, there is concern the river could erode and capture its main channel. The structure was nearly lost during the 1973 flood but was repaired and improved, with additional facilities increasing flow capacity and reducing future failure risks. The Morganza Spillway, located slightly higher and well back from the river, is normally dry; even if it fails at the crest during a severe flood, floodwaters would need to erode to normal levels before a permanent channel shift could occur. During the 2011 floods, the Corps of Engineers opened the Morganza Spillway to 1/4 of its capacity, releasing 150,000 cubic feet per second (4,200 m³/s) to flood the Morganza and Atchafalaya areas, reducing stress on the control system. Army Corps geologist Fred Smith stated that the river "wants to go west" and that a major flood—when structures can't release all water and the levee gives way—would cause the river to jump its banks. Another possible diversion is through Lake Pontchartrain near New Orleans, controlled by the Bonnet Carré Spillway and an imperfect natural levee 12–20 ft (3.7–6.1 m) high. A diversion through Lake Pontchartrain would have consequences similar to an Atchafalaya diversion but to a lesser extent, as the current channel would remain in use past Baton Rouge and into New Orleans. Water skiing was invented on the river in a wide region between Minnesota and Wisconsin.

The Old River Control Structure is a key feature in managing the Mississippi River's course, as Army Corps of Engineers geologist Fred Smith noted, "The Mississippi wants to go west." In 1973, a forty-year flood occurred, and a larger flood event—when the structures can't release all the floodwaters and the levee must give way—is expected to happen in the future, leading to the river jumping its banks and breaking through. Another potential course change involves a diversion into Lake Pontchartrain near New Orleans, which is currently prevented by the Bonnet Carré Spillway and an imperfect natural levee approximately 12–20 ft (3.7–6.1 m) high. If the Mississippi were to divert through Lake Pontchartrain, the consequences would resemble those of an Atchafalaya diversion but to a lesser extent, as the main river channel would continue to be used past Baton Rouge and into the New Orleans area. Water skiing was invented in a wide region between Minnesota and Wisconsin known as Lake Pepin, with Ralph Samuelson of Lake City, Minnesota, creating and refining his technique in late June and early July 1922. He performed the first water ski jump in 1925 and was pulled at 80 mph (130 km/h) by a Curtiss flying boat that same year. There are seven National Park Service sites along the Mississippi River, with the Mississippi National River and Recreation Area dedicated to protecting and interpreting the river itself. The other six sites are listed from north to south. The Mississippi basin supports a highly diverse aquatic fauna and is referred to as the "mother fauna" of North American freshwater. Approximately 375 fish species are known in the basin, surpassing other North Hemisphere river basins in temperate/subtropical regions except the Yangtze. Streams originating in the Appalachian and Ozark highlands contain especially high numbers of species, including numerous endemics and relicts such as paddlefish, sturgeon, gar, and bowfin. The Upper Mississippi River alone hosts about 120 fish species, including walleye, sauger, largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, white bass, northern pike, bluegill, crappie, channel catfish, flathead catfish, common shiner, freshwater drum, and shovelnose sturgeon. The basin is also home to many reptiles, including American alligators, various turtle species, aquatic amphibians, and cambaridae crayfish. About 40% of U.S. migratory birds use the Mississippi River corridor during spring and fall migrations, and 60% of all migratory birds in North America (326 species) use the river basin as a flyway. Numerous introduced species are present, including Asian carp such as silver carp, which have outcompeted native fish and are known for their dangerous jumping behavior and have spread widely throughout the basin, approaching but not yet invading the Great Lakes. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources has designated much of the Mississippi River in the state as infested with zebra mussels and Eurasian watermilfoil.
